Impulse Line Slope and Routing Rules by Service

An impulse line must slope so that unwanted fluid always drains back to the process or away from the instrument. The direction of slope depends on what can collect in the line: liquid in gas and steam service, or trapped gas in liquid service. A slope of about 1:10 to 1:12, roughly 5 to 10 degrees, is the typical figure, adjusted for fluid properties and condensation risk.

ServiceInstrument positionSlope directionWhat it prevents
GasAbove the process tappingDown toward the process lineCondensed liquid collecting in the line
LiquidBelow the process tappingDown toward the instrumentGas bubbles trapped in the line, which vent upward to the process
SteamBelow the tapping, with filled legsDown toward the instrumentUneven condensate legs and hot steam at the sensor
DP pairs, any serviceBoth lines routed togetherSame slope on HP and LPUnequal heads that shift the zero

Practical routing tips for every impulse line:

  1. Keep lines as short as possible and avoid high or low pockets.
  2. Run HP and LP lines side by side so they share the same temperature.
  3. Provide vents at high points and drains at low points.
  4. Support the tubing so the slope does not sag over time.
